info.bio: No Doubt (en español: sin duda) es una banda de Rock formada en 1986 en Anaheim, California, (Estados Unidos). Su música estuvo en sus inicios profundamente influenciada por el ska, evolucionando posteriormente más hacia el soft rock. También reciben influencia de los estilos reggae jamaicanos, habiendo actuado en múltiples ocasiones con artistas jamaicanos como Lady Saw. Fue 6 años después de su formación cuando lanzaron su álbum debut No Doubt

scenes.name: Hardcore en la era del punk-pop: emocore, ska-core y post-hardcore
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Mientras las revistas anuncian la «muerte del punk», el hardcore se convierte en un movimiento que no deja pueblo sin tocar y genera subgéneros. El «emocore» (Jawbreaker, Weezer, Sunny Day Real Estate, Promise Ring, At The Drive-In, Jimmy Eat World, Seaweed); el hardcore progresivo de Washington (Nation Of Ulysses, Make-Up, Shudder To Think, Jawbox, Edsel, Lungfish, Circus Lupus, Dismemberment Plan); el «ska-core» (Operation Ivy, Rancid, Mighty Mighty Bosstones, Sublime, No Doubt); el punk-pop que llega a las listas (Green Day, Offspring, Flop, Pennywise, Pegboy, Superchunk, Queers); el garage-punk californiano (Drive Like Jehu, Rocket From The Crypt, Blink 182, Zen Guerrilla); el jazzcore (Bazooka, Iceburn); la vieja escuela (D Generation, Supersuckers, Zeke, Dropkick Murphys, Silverfish, Turbonegro) y el post-hardcore de Unwound.
scenes.family: Punk, new wave, hardcore y noise

podcast.title: No Doubt (Anaheim, 1986) – Started as Applecore; Original Singer John Spence Committed Suicide Age 18; Tragic Kingdom (1995) 17 Million Copies; Eric Stefani Left for The Simpsons
podcast.body: No Doubt was formed in 1986 as a band called Applecore by Eric Stefani and his sister Gwen, later joined by John Spence (who said "no doubt" when he agreed with you — that became the band's name). Spence was the main singer with Gwen on backup. Just before a big showcase for major labels, Spence committed suicide at age 18. After a brief breakup, the band reformed with a new singer named Alan Mead, who didn't last, and then Gwen took over vocals. A self-titled 1992 album flopped (maybe 30,000 copies). A second album called The Beacon Street Collection sold only a few more. Keyboardist Eric Stefani then left to become an animator for The Simpsons, preferring animation to music. Interscope paired the remaining band with producer Matthew Wilder; the resulting Tragic Kingdom came out October 10, 1995 and eventually sold north of 17 million copies worldwide, doing more for ska punk than any other CD. "At last count worldwide sales were somewhere north of 17 million copies."

"and a new group from Orange County called No Doubt."

podcast.title: Relationship, Breakup, and Band Success
podcast.body: Gwen Stefani and Tony Canal of No Doubt were in a romantic relationship that eventually ended. Despite their breakup, they successfully continued as bandmates through the band's most successful period in the 1980s. "Gwen Stefani and Tony Canal from No Doubt, they were in a relationship but then broke up, yet were able to hold it together as the band went through their most successful period back in the 1980s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reunion for Touring
podcast.body: No Doubt was one of many bands from past decades that reunited in the 21st century, a trend largely motivated by financial incentives. With declining CD sales impacting artist revenues, returning to the touring circuit offered a lucrative way to appeal to nostalgic fan bases and fill large venues. "The list of reunions is long."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 1: (100-91)

podcast.title: Third Wave Mainstream Breakthrough
podcast.body: No Doubt, based out of Orange County, struggled through two albums before their 1995 album "Tragic Kingdom" brought them mainstream success. They adopted a new wave sound combined with the Ska beat, diverging from the more common punk or metal direction of many third-wave Ska bands. "The first third wave act to really break through into the mainstream was one that we also talked about during the chapter on punk rock revivals."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Third Wave Ska Leader
podcast.body: No Doubt was a prominent band in the "third wave" of Ska, which arrived in the 1990s. This wave saw significant popularity with bands like The Mighty Mighty Bosstones, Sublime, Reel Big Fish, Goldfinger, and Dance Hall Crashers. The Interrupters were noted as the first female-fronted Ska band to have a major hit since No Doubt. "Third wave Scott arrived in the 1990s, no doubt, muddy, muddy boss tones, sublime, real big fish, gold finger, dancehall crashes and so many more." "They became the first female fronted Skaban to have a major hit since no doubt."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tom's Demand for Hiatus (2004)
xref.body: At the end of the No Doubt tour, Tom decided he "didn't need this crap anymore" and demanded six months off, citing a need for more family time, which was problematic given a major US tour and charity event commitments. "At the end of that no doubt tour, Tom decided he didn't need this crap anymore. He demanded six months off. I need more time with my family, he said."

xref.title: Aftermath of Toronto Stage Collapse
xref.body: The Toronto show was canceled, and Scott Johnson's death devastated everyone involved. The incident led to a prolonged and unresolved legal process, including investigations, lawsuits, counter-suits, charges against Live Nation, Optics Staging and Services, and engineer Dominic Caligari (all pleaded not guilty), two criminal trials, and a mistrial. As of the end of 2018, no one had been held accountable, and no inquest had been conducted. Scott Johnson's father, Ken Johnson, an expert in scaffolding health and safety, had "no doubt why the accident happened." "And then came the long, farcical train of investigations, lawsuits, counter-suits, charges, switch judges, legal bureaucracies, two criminal trials, and in the end, a mistrial that left everything unresolved."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Desert Session Projects – Produced by Eleven Members
xref.body: Josh Homme's Desert Session projects received production assistance from Elaine Johannes and Natasha Schneider of the band Eleven, following their work on Chris Cornell's solo album. This collaboration brought Johannes and Schneider into contact with members from various other prominent bands, including A Perfect Circle, Nine Inch Nails, Danzig, Marilyn Manson's band, and PJ Harvey. "got producing gigs for no doubt in Josh Hommie in the early days of his desert session projects, which brought them into contact with members of a perfect circle, nine-inch nails, Danzig, Wade, Maryland Manson's band, and PJ Harvey."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: First Female-Fronted Ska Band with Major Hit Since No Doubt
xref.body: The Interrupters were highlighted as a significant band in the "fourth wave" of Ska, which arrived in the late 2010s. They became the first female-fronted Ska band to achieve a major hit since No Doubt, showcasing the genre's continued evolution and relevance in North America. "If you're into the scene, you might know about the steady 45s, lost agritones and of course, the interruptors." "They became the first female fronted Skaban to have a major hit since no doubt."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 4: The Revivals

xref.title: Fourth Wave Leader
xref.body: The Interrupters, from Los Angeles, record for Hellcat Records (a label associated with Rancid) and are considered the current leader in the fourth wave of Ska. Their success marks the first female-fronted Ska hit since No Doubt. "The biggest of them all, so far, has been the Interruptors. They're from Los Angeles and record for Hellcat Records, a label associated with, and here's that name again, Ranset. This was the first female fronted SCAT hit, since no doubt. The Interruptors, the current leader in the 4th wave of SCAT."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Producers for Chris Cornell's Solo Album – Launchpad for Other Gigs
xref.body: The group Eleven, comprising Elaine Johannes and Natasha Schneider, played a crucial role in producing Chris Cornell's debut solo record, *Euphoria Morning*. Their work on this album garnered them further producing gigs for notable artists like No Doubt and Josh Homme's Desert Session projects, connecting them to members of A Perfect Circle, Nine Inch Nails, Danzig, Marilyn Manson's band, and PJ Harvey. "Chris reliant on both of them to help produce his debut solo record Euphoria Morning... who, based on this work, got producing gigs for no doubt in Josh Hommie in the early days of his desert session projects."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Solo Career and Philanthropy
xref.body: In addition to selling over 35 million records with No Doubt, Gwen Stefani sold millions more as a solo artist. She raised millions of dollars for child victims of the 2011 tsunami in Japan and supports various LGBT organizations and causes. "She sold over 35 million records with no doubt and millions more as a solo artist. She's raised millions of dollars for child victims of the 2011 tsunami in Japan. She supports various LGBT organizations and causes."
